name: What to Measure
title: What to Measure
answer: The most common AI pilot measures, such as logins, minutes of use and prompt counts, only show that a tool was opened, not that anything improved. A pilot should instead measure the problem it was meant to solve, whether that is teacher time saved or learning on a task done without the tool. Every pilot should also count governance incidents, because a tool that works but causes harm is not a success.

sections.body: This idea is about choosing what to measure in an AI pilot, because the usual measures are the least useful. Logins, minutes of use and prompt counts prove only that people opened the tool, and a tool can be used constantly with no effect on learning or workload. High usage can even hide the problem of students leaning on the tool and learning less. The right measures follow from the problem the pilot was meant to solve, so a time-saving goal calls for minutes saved per week and a learning goal calls for learning measured without the tool. Most pilots should pick one main measure and one or two supporting ones, and all should count governance incidents.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, the measure is set by the goal of the pilot. If the goal was saving teacher time, the pilot measures minutes saved per week and then asks where those minutes went. If the goal was learning, the pilot measures learning on a task done without the tool and compares it with a classroom that did not use it. The text does not give separate grade bands for this idea. Figure 4.6 lists eight kinds of measures with an example of each, and most pilots should choose one main measure and one or two supporting ones. Every pilot should also count governance incidents such as privacy problems or reports of harm.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book's evidence label for this idea is not stated as a single label, but it cites specific findings. One study found that teachers who cut their planning time in half saw the saved time absorbed by other demands (Carson et al., 2026). A review of automatic feedback found that nearly half of the studies showed no reduction in teacher workload at all (Cavalcanti et al., 2021). A review of AI in math found an average effect that researchers classify as small (Yi et al., 2024), and realistic effects are usually small. A small effect can still be worth having, especially at low cost, but it needs to be measured honestly rather than assumed.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits start with the measures themselves: logins, minutes of use and prompt counts show only that a tool was opened, and high usage can mask students learning less. A tool that works but causes harm is not a success, whatever its other numbers say, so every pilot should count governance incidents such as privacy problems or reports of harm. The decisions about which problem the pilot is meant to solve, which main measure and supporting measures to use, and where saved teacher time actually goes stay with the people running the pilot. The text does not set out further limits or decision rights beyond these.
